seo.title: Karmic tail 3 7 4 compatibility: who rules in the couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 3 7 4 compatibility: the Empress, the Chariot and the Emperor. A couple that wants a shared garden, travels apart and has to learn to share power.

title: Karmic tail 3-7-4 in compatibility: the Empress, the Chariot and the Emperor
short: The couple's tail 3-7-4 looks like a ready-made equation: the Empress plus the Emperor equals the Chariot. In this compatibility karmic tail the couple enters the task through a wish for a shared garden and plenty, lives it out on the road, where each partner drives a chariot of their own, and arrives at the main lesson: agreeing on power — who rules what in the couple, and how to keep a promise without letting it become a chain.

sections.h2: How the 3-7-4 tail is formed: two royal cards in the middles
paragraphs: Every point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The entry to the task is the sum of the two personal entries, the middle is the sum of the two personal middles, and the main task is the sum of the two karmic tasks. This is how it looks for the dates 02.01.1980 and 14.10.1975.

The partners' personal tails are 9-3-21 and 21-4-10. This is not a quirk of the example: a check of every date shows that the couple's tail 3-7-4 is built only from these two personal tails, in 100% of such couples. There is no other way to reach it.

Now look at the middles. The person with the tail 9-3-21 has the Empress in the middle; the person with 21-4-10 has the Emperor. The couple's tail begins with that same Empress, ends with that same Emperor, and in its middle stands the Chariot, made of both: 3 + 4 = 7. **The two royal cards the partners carry inside their own tails stand at the two ends of the couple's road, and in the middle of it they ride in one chariot.**

This does not mean that one of the two is "the Emperor" and the other "the Empress". Sex has no effect on the numbers, and the middle of a personal tail is not a role in the couple. The coincidence says something else: both kinds of power, the soft and the firm, are present in this couple from the first day, and the main task is not to choose one of them but to bring them together into a shared order.

The centre works the same way. With the tail 21-4-10 the personal centre is always 11, Strength; with 9-3-21 it is always 6, the Lovers. Their sum is 17, the Star, and it stands in the centre of 100% of couples with this tail. Neither partner has the Star in the centre, and neither can: no date of birth ever gives 17 in the centre of a personal matrix. This card appears only when the two are counted together.

Nor does 3-7-4 exist as a personal tail. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre, and with a task of 4 an entry of 3 is impossible whatever the centre. No other couple's tail is made of the numbers 3, 7 and 4: this triple occurs only in this order. The tail appears in about one couple in 217 (0.461%), which puts it 58th of the 97 couple's tails.

sections.h2: The Franklin's Tale: a marriage that began with an agreement about power
paragraphs: In Chaucer's Canterbury Tales (late fourteenth century) pilgrims take turns telling stories, and several stories in a row argue about one thing: who should have the upper hand in marriage. The Wife of Bath demands power for the wife; meek Griselda in the Clerk's Tale endures any will of her husband's. In 1912 the American scholar George Lyman Kittredge read these tales as a single debate on marriage, and they have been called the "Marriage Group" ever since. The Franklin's Tale is usually read as the answer to the whole debate.

The teller himself seems to be made of two of our cards. In the General Prologue we learn that in the Franklin's house "it snewed ... of mete and drinke" — it snowed food and drink — and that his table stood laid in the hall all day long, while at the court sessions "ther was he lord and sire"; he had been a sheriff and sat as knight of the shire. A host of plenty and a man of power in one person. Even his title speaks of freedom: a franklin is a free landholder, from Old French franc, "free". Keep that word in mind: the tale will end on it.

The Franklin claims to be retelling an old Breton lay. In fact the nearest source is Boccaccio: a question of love in Book IV of the Filocolo (the 1330s) and the fifth story of the tenth day of the Decameron. The root of the plot is older still, and Indian: in the Vetala tales about a girl who made a rash promise, the same final question is asked — which of the three was the most generous. Here and below Chaucer is quoted in the original Middle English from Skeat's edition, with plain glosses where needed; Boccaccio is quoted in our own translation from the Italian.

The story goes like this. In Brittany the knight Arveragus long courts the noble lady Dorigen, and she agrees to marry him. Then Chaucer does something Boccaccio does not: before telling us about the marriage, he spells out its contract. Of his own free will Arveragus swears never to take mastery over his wife against her will, never to show jealousy, and to obey her in everything, as a lover obeys his lady — **"save that the name of soveraynetee"**, the name of sovereignty, which he will keep for himself "for shame of his degree". Dorigen answers that since he offers her "so large a reyne", such a loose rein, she will be his humble, true wife. And the Franklin adds a word of his own:

"Frendes everich other moot obeye, if they wol longe holden companye. Love wol nat ben constreyned by maistrye; whan maistrie comth, the god of love anon beteth hise winges, and farewel! he is gon! Love is a thing as any spirit free; wommen of kinde desiren libertee, and nat to ben constreyned as a thral; and so don men, if I soth seyen shal" (lines 762–770).

The contract ends in "an humble wys accord": she has taken him as both servant and lord — "servant in love, and lord in mariage". It is hard to imagine a better agreement. The 3-7-4 tail begins with exactly such an agreement, and the whole tale tests whether it will survive the road.

The tail fits the tale almost act by act. The Empress is the first year of marriage and the garden in May. The Chariot is the husband's departure in search of glory and everything that happens while he is away. The Emperor is his return and the decision he takes for both of them. And in the middle of the plot, where the couple has the Star in its centre, sits an astrologer from Orléans, counting the stars.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — the Empress: a garden asked for in January
paragraphs: Point M in a couple's tail is what the two want together: shared wishes, agreements, a common language. Here the Empress is the wish to live in plenty: a home of their own, a generous table, a garden, children or a joint venture, prosperity that can be seen. Chaucer describes the first years of such a couple in a single line: who could tell, unless he had been married, "the joye, the ese, and the prosperitee that is bitwixe an housbonde and his wyf"? The last of those words is the Empress's own: plenty that keeps growing. For a year and more Arveragus and Dorigen live "in blisse and in solas". This is the Empress at the entry: the two are happy together, and everything around them grows.

But the entry of the tail stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish can turn into resistance. With the Empress the resistance looks soft: agree "out of love" without spelling anything out; give the reins a little more slack; hurt nobody with a refusal. That is exactly how trouble begins in Chaucer. In a garden on "the sixte morwe of May", a garden like no other "but-if it were the verray paradys", the young neighbour Aurelius confesses his love to Dorigen. She answers firmly: never. Then, seeing how he suffers, she adds — "in pley", Chaucer stresses — that she will love him if he clears every rock from the coast of Brittany, stone by stone. **"For wel I woot that it shal never bityde."**

In Boccaccio the same scene comes even closer to the Empress. The lady of the Filocolo wants to be rid of a persistent suitor and asks for an impossible gift: "in the month of January, in this land, a fine large garden, full of grass and flowers and trees and fruit, as if it were May". And she tells herself: "This is impossible — that is how I will get him off my back." In the Decameron Madonna Dianora asks for the same thing — a garden in January as lovely as in May. Chaucer swapped the garden for the rocks, but the motif stayed: the wish that it should always be May turns into a promise that someone will one day come to collect.

In a couple with the 3-7-4 tail this mechanism is easy to recognise. One partner cannot say "no" without softening it — "well, unless…" — and the softening sounds like a promise. The other agrees to a move, a loan, a joint business "some day", because right now it seems impossible. While it is May in the house, such words cost nothing. The task of the entry is to speak about wishes directly and not to hand out promises that rest only on the certainty that they will never have to be kept.

sections.h2: Middle of the task — the Chariot: two years in England and the black rocks
paragraphs: In Lisovskaya's book point N has no meaning of its own: it is an addition to the main task. We read it as the road — what the couple does and goes through on the way from the wish to the task. In the 3-7-4 tail that road is the Chariot: movement, a road of one's own for each, a race of one's own and victories of one's own.

In Chaucer the Chariot begins a year after the wedding. Arveragus leaves for England "to seke in armes worship and honour; for al his lust he sette in swich labour" — all his delight was in such labour — and stays there two years. He writes letters home, doubts nothing, and on his return "no-thing list him to been imaginatyf": he has no wish to imagine whether anyone spoke of love to his wife while he was away. Dorigen, meanwhile, weeps, lies awake, walks with her friends along the high shore counting ships — and every time she looks down she sees the "grisly rokkes blake" on which his ship might break.

Her prayer on the shore is already about the main task of the tail: "Eterne god, that thurgh thy purveyaunce ledest the world by certein governaunce" — eternal God, who guides the world by sure governance — why did you make these rocks, which do nobody any good? The one who stayed at home argues about who rules the world and how, while the one who left seeks glory in arms. **The Chariot in the middle of the tail divides the couple like this: one gets the road and the glory, the other the shore and the fear.** Each sees their own: the one who travels does not see the rocks, and the one who waits sees nothing else.

In a modern couple this is rotation work, a long project, study in another city, a start-up that eats every evening, or simply working "until the last". Or both are in chariots — and then the argument is about whose road matters more, who will adjust and who will give way first. Among the tasks of a couple with the Chariot, Lisovskaya names the balance between career and relationship and the rivalry for leadership. The bright side of the Chariot is visible in Chaucer too: Arveragus is not jealous, he keeps his vow never to "kythe hir jalousye", and the letters keep coming home. The Chariot does not have to separate — it has to come back.

In Boccaccio the middle of the plot is a chariot in the literal sense. The suitor has searched the whole West for a sorcerer and finds him in Thessaly: a poor old man called Tebano, gathering herbs. At night Tebano stretches out his arms to the stars, calls on the night, the stars, Hecate and Ceres for help — and "the stars did not shine in vain: swifter than the flight of any bird a chariot drawn by two dragons came before him; he mounted it, took the reins in his hands and rose into the air". For three days he flies over mountains and rivers, cutting herbs, and the dragons, breathing in their scent, shed their old skins and grow young again. The Chariot gives strength back to the one who drives it towards a goal rather than away from something.

One more detail. Chaucer's marriage contract is phrased from the start in the language of harness: Dorigen thanks her husband for letting the reins run so loose. The question of who holds the reins stands at this couple's entry, is settled on the road, and becomes the main task at the end.

sections.h2: Main task — the Emperor: "Is ther oght elles, Dorigen, but this?"
paragraphs: Point D is the couple's main task: what does not work for it and what it has to learn; it is read above all through the shadow side. The Emperor in this point means power, order, rules, responsibility. On the shadow side: decisions made for everyone, rigidity, rules that later get in the way of the very people who made them, and a face on which nobody can tell joy from anger. On the bright side: support and protection, an agreement on boundaries that lets both feel safe.

In Chaucer the task arrives in a single evening. For two years Aurelius lies "in langour and in torment"; then his brother takes him to a learned astrologer in Orléans. For a thousand pounds of gold the man undertakes to remove the rocks, arrives in Brittany in "the colde frosty seson of Decembre", and makes it so that "for a wyke or tweye, it semed that alle the rokkes were aweye". Aurelius comes to Dorigen: "wel I woot the rokkes been aweye!" For two days she weeps alone — her husband is away from home — and on the third night Arveragus returns and asks why she is crying. She tells him everything.

The husband's first words are the Emperor at his best. He answers "with glad chere, in freendly wyse": **"Is ther oght elles, Dorigen, but this?"** — is there anything else, Dorigen, but this? And then: "lat slepen that is stille" — let sleeping dogs lie; it may yet turn out well. No shouting, no accusation, no jealous scene. His next words are the Emperor's shadow, in the same minute: "Ye shul your trouthe holden, by my fay! … Trouthe is the hyeste thing that man may kepe." With that word he burst into tears and said: "I yow forbede, up peyne of deeth" — on pain of death — ever to tell anyone of this; he would bear his grief as best he could and show no sign of sorrow, so that people should think no harm of her. A squire and a maid take her towards the garden; nobody knows why.

The man who at the wedding gave up power over his wife against her will gives an order for the first time in a crisis. The "name of sovereignty", kept for other people's eyes, turns into sovereignty overnight. And everything in his decision is noble: he puts his wife's word above his own pain, guards her good name, hides his tears. But the decision is taken for two, the rule is placed above the person, and the grief is hidden for the sake of onlookers. Chaucer himself expects the listeners' indignation: "Paraventure an heep of yow, y-wis, wol holden him a lewed man in this, that he wol putte his wyf in jupartye; herkneth the tale, er ye up-on hir crye" — perhaps many of you will think him a fool for putting his wife in jeopardy; hear the tale before you cry out against her.

This is what the main task of 3-7-4 looks like in everyday life. The couple agreed that each decides for themselves — until the first crisis, when one suddenly decides for both, "for our sake". Someone once said in passing, "your parents are your business", "we each keep our own money", "if it comes to that, we split without drama" — and a rule spoken in May starts being carried out to the letter in December. In public they keep up appearances; at home they do not talk about what matters. Among Lisovskaya's tasks for a couple with the Emperor there are two that read like a summary of Chaucer: **do not create rules that later get in the way, and learn to talk about feelings.**

In Boccaccio the husband's act is judged by a court of love. Queen Fiammetta finds a legal answer: at the wedding both partners swear to be content with each other, and "no later oath can override the first one lawfully made". So the wife's promise to her suitor was worthless from the start. The verdict translates easily into a couple's language. Sooner or later any two people make promises on the side — to work, to parents, to friends, to the bank, to themselves. The main task of the tail is to know which agreement comes first, and not to let a later one cancel an earlier one.

Her companion Menedon objects with a phrase that suits a couple with the Emperor as their main task very well: "whoever gives what he cannot refuse gives little". A concession made by the rule is not yet a gift.

sections.h2: The Chariot in Waite and Wen: two powers in one carriage
paragraphs: Put the three cards of the tail side by side in the books, and the coincidences become almost awkward. Waite describes the Empress and the Emperor as a pair: the Emperor is "by imputation the spouse of the former", and he adds at once that the two cards "do not precisely represent the condition of married life, though this state is implied". In the 3-7-4 tail the couple travels from one of them to the other.

The Chariot between them is, for Waite, "really the King in his triumph", "typifying, however, the victory which creates kingship as its natural consequence and not the vested royalty of the fourth card". In this tail the seventh card leads straight to the fourth: the couple wins first and then learns to rule. Waite's chariot is drawn by two sphinxes, Boccaccio's by two dragons: two forces in one harness.

The most precise clue is in Benebell Wen. The chariot, she writes, bears a badge with the lingam and the yoni — Shiva and Shakti — and its traditional meaning is **"the union of the external sphere of rulership by man and the internal sphere of rulership by woman"**. Two powers in one carriage: exactly what the tail builds from the Emperor and the Empress. The split by sex is an old tradition here, not a rule for the couple: Chaucer's knight himself hands power to his wife and keeps only the name. The question of the 3-7-4 tail is not which sphere belongs to whom by birth, but who rules what by agreement.

In Wen both of them hold a sign of power. The Empress "holds up her baton of sovereignty"; for the Emperor, "the scepter or crux ansata is his sovereignty; the orb is his dominion". The soft power of plenty and the firm power of order are both power, not power and submission. Sovereignty, soveraynetee, is the very word Arveragus kept for himself "in name".
One last detail will matter when we come to the stars: in Waite the arms of the Emperor's throne "are fronted by rams' heads", and Wen links the card to the sign of Aries.

sections.h2: The Star in the centre: what the astrologer from Orléans measured by the stars
paragraphs: The couple's centre is its shared atmosphere, what lies between the two and is not on show. In every couple with the 3-7-4 tail it holds the Star — a card no single person ever has in the centre. In Lisovskaya's reading, the Star in a couple's centre at its best is a union that inspires both partners: they say plainly what they like and what they do not, they know how to forgive, and the beautiful picture, for once, turns out to be true. On the shadow side: things left unsaid, a showy wrapping, ultimatums.

In the middle of the Franklin's Tale stands a man with the stars. The astrologer from Orléans brings out his "tables Toletanes", works out the mansions of the moon and, as Chaucer puts it, "knew ful wel how fer Alnath was shove fro the heed of thilke fixe Aries above that in the ninthe speere considered is" — how far the star Alnath had been pushed from the head of the fixed Aries of the ninth sphere. This is a calculation of precession: the stars slowly drift away from the point they were once fixed to. Just before this the Franklin assures us, "I ne can no termes of astrologye" — I know no terms of astrology — and then pours them out. Chaucer knew them perfectly well: in 1391 he wrote a treatise on the astrolabe for his little son Lewis.

**Our own observation, not a teaching of the sources: the astrologer measures the distance between a star and the Ram — between the card in this couple's centre and the sign of its main task.** That is exactly what a couple with the 3-7-4 tail has to do from time to time: check how far their shared star — hope, inspiration, faith in each other — has drifted from the fixed point of their first agreement. Not to drag it back into place by force, but to know where it stands now.

The Star's shadow is in this story too. The rocks did not vanish — they only "semed" to be gone for a week or two. An atmosphere of hope is good at producing appearances: "it will work out somehow", "that will never happen", "everything is fine with us". And right beside it is the Star at its best: Dorigen tells her husband everything, hiding nothing. The trouble will end precisely because the truth was spoken aloud — and nearly begins again when the husband forbids her to speak it to anyone else.

Waite gives the Star two mottoes: "Waters of Life freely" and "Gifts of the Spirit". Wen calls it "a card of divine charity": it is about "giving more than the Seeker receives". In Boccaccio, Menedon speaks of generosity in words that sound like a description of this card: "it is a great thing to bear a long thirst, reach the fountain and not drink, so as to let another drink". And the Franklin said before his story had even begun: "Love is a thing as any spirit free." In the centre of this couple stands a card of the gift — and, as the ending will show, it is the gift, not the rule, that solves the main task.

sections.h2: The couple's values: free choice or bonds
paragraphs: The couple's spiritual purpose is its values, what the union exists for. Couples with the 3-7-4 tail have one of two cards there: the Lovers (6) in 59% and the Devil (15) in 41%. Both answer the question of the main task, only from different sides.

The Lovers are the value of choice. What matters to such a couple is that the two choose each other again and again, and every rule is tested by one thing: does it take that choice away? For them the Franklin's line is almost a charter: love will not be constrained by mastery, and when mastery comes, the god of love flies off. Such a couple needs the Emperor of its main task as a frame in which choice can live, not as a lock on the door.

The Devil is the value of bonds, of what ties people together. Such couples are held by promises, shared debts and obligations, an attachment that is hard to break. In Chaucer the bonds are literally visible: Dorigen complains to Fortune, who has "unwar wrapped" her "in thy cheyne", Aurelius owes the astrologer a thousand pounds of gold, and the resolution sounds like a legal formula: "I yow relesse, madame, in-to your hond quit every surement and every bond." Lisovskaya ends her chapter on the Devil with the thought that nobody belongs to anybody. For such a couple the main task is to keep the bonds a union and not let them become a chain.

sections.h2: Who was the most generous: how the 3-7-4 tail opens up at its best
paragraphs: Chaucer's ending is a chain of releases. Aurelius meets Dorigen in the street; she is going "un-to the gardin, as myn housbond bad, my trouthe for to holde, allas! allas!". Seeing her grief and her husband's nobility, he lets her go: "and right as frely as he sente hir me, as frely sente I hir to him ageyn". The astrologer, hearing of this, forgives Aurelius the debt: shall a clerk not do a noble deed as well as a knight and a squire? The Franklin ends with a question to his listeners: **"Which was the moste free, as thinketh yow?"** The man whose title means "free" asks who was the freest of them all.

People have answered the question in different ways. Boccaccio's Fiammetta names the husband: he gave away the dearest thing, his honour. Menedon disagrees: the sorcerer was the most generous, because the old man returned of his own will to poverty. The king in the Indian Vetala tale thinks the thief was the noble one. The cards of the 3-7-4 tail answer differently: **in this couple power is settled not by whoever holds the rule most tightly, but by whoever lets go first.** Waite's Emperor reversed means "benevolence, compassion, credit", and the tale ends with exactly that: Aurelius's compassion and the respite on his debt, which the astrologer turns into forgiveness.
What helps a couple with this tail live it at its best:

ul: **Agree on power aloud and by area.** Who decides about money, the home, moving, children or the joint venture — and make sure the "name of sovereignty" shown to relatives and friends does not differ from how things really work at home.
**Make no promises "in jest"** or "because it will never happen": the impossible does sometimes happen, and someone comes to collect.
**Talk about the rocks before the journey.** Before a departure, a new job or a big project, discuss what frightens the one who stays, not only what the one who goes stands to win.
**In a hard moment, start with a question, not a decision:** "is there anything else but this?" — and decide together, even if one of you is sure they know the nobler way.
**Do not hide grief for the sake of other people's opinion.** An Emperor who keeps up a face for the public is left alone with his throne.
**Check the star against the Ram.** From time to time revisit the first agreement: not "but we agreed", but "where are we now compared with what we agreed".

paragraphs: Chaucer's last lines about the couple are the strong version of this tail: "Arveragus and Dorigene his wyf in sovereyn blisse leden forth hir lyf. Never eft ne was ther angre hem bitwene; he cherisseth hir as though she were a quene; and she was to him trewe for evermore." The road from the Empress to the Emperor closes on the Empress, but now she is crowned not by the softness of a May agreement but by an order tested in winter. The garden that Boccaccio's sorcerer raised by magic in January, such a couple can grow itself: **plenty that rests not on an endless May but on an agreement that has come through December.**

ul: **3 — The Empress, entry to the task.** The shared wish: a home, a generous table, a joint venture, a life where there is enough of everything. The same wish for softness turns into resistance when the time comes to agree on something seriously.
**7 — The Chariot, middle of the task.** How the couple moves towards its goal: in motion, often apart, with departures, races and an argument about who holds the reins.
**4 — The Emperor, main task.** What the couple has to learn: power shared by two — rules that suit both, and decisions that are not taken on the other's behalf, even out of nobility.

intro: The equation 3 + 4 = 7 only looks simple. The middle of a couple's tail is not worked out from its two ends: it is the sum of the middles of two personal tails, and those middles hold exactly the same two cards — the Emperor in one person's tail and the Empress in the other's. And the plot of this tail was written, almost scene by scene, more than six hundred years ago: in Geoffrey Chaucer's Franklin's Tale a marriage begins with an agreement about power and ends with the question of who was the most generous of all.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 3-7-4 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail: the Empress at the entry to the task, the Chariot in the middle and the Emperor as the main task. The couple wants shared plenty and a home, travels towards it through movement, departures and races, and has to learn power shared by two — agreements that suit both, and decisions that are not taken on the other's behalf.

faq.q: Is the 3-7-4 tail a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail describes a task, not a verdict and not a forecast. It shows where such a couple stumbles — soft promises, separate roads and decisions made for two — and what it can learn. The main task is read through its shadow side because it is a lesson, not a judgement of the union.

faq.q: Why do couples with the 3-7-4 tail always have the Star in the centre?
faq.a: The 3-7-4 tail is built only from the personal tails 21-4-10 and 9-3-21. With the first the personal centre is always 11, Strength; with the second always 6, the Lovers; and 11 + 6 = 17. No date of birth gives the Star in the centre of a personal matrix, so a couple receives this card only as two.

faq.q: Can 3-7-4 be a personal karmic tail?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre, and with a task of 4 an entry of 3 is impossible whatever the centre. So 3-7-4 is only a couple's tail, and texts about personal tails do not apply to it: the calculation and the points are different.

faq.q: Who is "the Emperor" in a couple with the 3-7-4 tail?
faq.a: Nobody by appointment. One partner has the Emperor in the middle of their personal tail and the other has the Empress, but that is about numbers, not about who leads. Sex does not affect the calculation. The main task is shared: both have to learn a kind of power that keeps order without taking away the other's voice.

In everyday life this is "well, unless…" instead of a plain "no", or agreeing to a move or a joint business "some day", because right now it seems impossible. While it is May in the house, such words cost nothing.

report.h3: One gets the road, the other the rocks

report: A year later the husband leaves for England "to seke in armes worship and honour" and stays there two years. He writes letters and doubts nothing. His wife counts ships from the high shore and sees below the "grisly rokkes blake" on which his ship might break. Her prayer there is already about the main task: why did God, who guides the world "by certein governaunce", make these rocks at all?

**The Chariot in the middle of the tail divides the couple like this: one gets the road and the glory, the other the shore and the fear.** The one who travels does not see the rocks; the one who waits sees nothing else. In a modern couple this is a long project, rotation work, study in another city — or two chariots at once and an argument about whose road matters more. The Chariot does not have to separate — it has to come back. It is no accident that Chaucer's marriage contract is phrased in the language of harness: the wife thanks her husband for letting the reins run so loose.

report.h3: "Is ther oght elles, Dorigen, but this?"

report: The astrologer from Orléans makes it so that for a week or two the rocks "semed" to be gone. Dorigen tells her husband everything. His first words are the Emperor at his best: **"Is ther oght elles, Dorigen, but this?"** — is there anything else, Dorigen, but this? No shouting, no jealousy. His next words are the Emperor's shadow, in the same minute: "Trouthe is the hyeste thing that man may kepe." He burst into tears, forbade her "up peyne of deeth" ever to tell anyone, and promised to show no sign of sorrow, so that people should think no harm of her.

The man who gave up power over his wife gives an order for the first time in a crisis. Everything in his decision is noble, but the decision is taken for two, the rule is placed above the person, and the grief is hidden for the sake of onlookers. In everyday life this is "each of us decides for ourselves" — until the first crisis, when one decides for both, "for our sake"; a rule dropped in passing in May that is carried out to the letter in December. The couple's main task is to create no rules that later get in the way, and to learn to talk about feelings. In Boccaccio a court of love adds that no later oath can override the first one lawfully made. The couple needs to know which of its agreements comes first.

Benebell Wen sees on the Chariot a badge that traditionally stands for the union of two spheres of rulership, the external and the internal. Two powers in one carriage — exactly what this tail is made of. The question is not which sphere belongs to whom, but who rules what by agreement.

report.h3: A star checked against the Ram

report: A couple with this tail always has the Star in the centre — a card no single person ever has there: only two people together can produce it. At the centre of the tale stands a man with the stars as well. The astrologer works out "how fer Alnath was shove fro the heed of thilke fixe Aries", how far the star Alnath had drifted from the head of the fixed Ram, and in Wen the Ram is the Emperor's sign. This is our own observation, not a teaching of the sources, but it is exactly the work the couple has to do: from time to time, check how far their shared hope has drifted from the point of their first agreement.

The ending is a chain of releases. The neighbour lets Dorigen go once he sees her grief: "and right as frely as he sente hir me, as frely sente I hir to him ageyn". The astrologer forgives him the debt. The Franklin, whose title means "free", asks his listeners "which was the moste free". **In this couple power is settled not by whoever holds the rule most tightly, but by whoever lets go first.**
What helps a couple live this tail at its best:

ul: agreeing on power aloud and by area — money, the home, moving, children or the joint venture;
making no promises "in jest" or "because it will never happen";
talking about the rocks before the journey, not after it;
in a hard moment, starting with a question rather than a decision, and deciding together;
not hiding grief for the sake of other people's opinion.

report: Chaucer's last lines about the couple: "Never eft ne was ther angre hem bitwene; he cherisseth hir as though she were a quene." The road from the Empress to the Emperor comes back to the Empress. Boccaccio's January garden was raised by magic, but such a couple can grow one itself: **plenty that rests not on an endless May but on an agreement that has come through December.**

unit.title: A pact that outlasted December

captions.M: To want a shared garden, a home and plenty
captions.N: To each drive your own road and come back
captions.D: To share power and keep your word without chains

unit.meaning: Your task is to agree on which of you rules what, and in hard moments to decide together, not for the other.
